key_terms.meaning: A pulse of unit area and vanishing width; its Laplace transform is 1, so it contains all frequencies equally.
Zero for t < 0 and one for t ≥ 0; Laplace transform 1/s; the standard command for position.
Rises at 1 unit per second; reaches 1 at t = 1 s; Laplace transform 1/s²; the standard command for velocity.
t²/2 for t ≥ 0, a constant acceleration of 1 unit/s²; Laplace transform 1/s³; the standard command for acceleration.
Number of poles of the open-loop transfer function G(s), equal to the degree of the characteristic polynomial; an n-pole system has order n.
Number of poles of G(s) lying at the origin s = 0; written type 0, type 1, type 2, and it alone fixes the steady-state error.
The number in G(s) = K/(1 + τs); the output of a first-order system reaches 63.2% of its final value at t = τ seconds.
The undamped oscillation frequency of a second-order system, in rad/s; it sets the speed of the response.
A dimensionless number that sets the shape of the second-order response; ζ = 0, 0 < ζ < 1, ζ = 1 and ζ > 1 give four different shapes.
ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) rad/s, the actual frequency at which an underdamped system oscillates.
0 < ζ < 1; the response overshoots the final value and then oscillates while decaying.
ζ = 1; the response reaches the final value as fast as possible without any overshoot.
ζ > 1; the response rises slowly with no oscillation, like two first-order systems in cascade.
For underdamped systems, the time to go from 0 to 100% of the final value; it is (π − β)/ωd, where β = cos⁻¹ ζ.
Time of the first peak of the response; t_p = π/ωd seconds for a second-order system.
M_p = 100·e^(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)) percent, the height of the first peak above the final value.
Time after which the response stays inside a band of 2% (or 5%) of the final value; t_s ≈ 4/(ζωn) seconds for the 2% band.

key_terms.term: Static error constants K_p, K_v, K_a
key_terms.meaning: K_p = lim(s→0) G(s), K_v = lim(s→0) sG(s), K_a = lim(s→0) s²G(s); they give the steady-state error for step, ramp and parabolic inputs.
Expansion of E(s)/R(s) about s = 0 as C₀ + C₁s + C₂s² + …, which gives the error for any slowly varying input.
The numbers C₀, C₁, C₂, … read off the generalized error series; each multiplies one derivative of the input in the time-domain error formula.

takeaways: Four ideal inputs — impulse, step, ramp, parabola — let every system be compared under the same conditions, because the response to one of them plus superposition gives the response to any input.
Order decides how many state variables and what shape the transient has; type decides only what error remains after the transient ends.
For a first-order system one number, τ, tells everything: 63.2% at τ, about 95% at 3τ, about 98% at 4τ.
A second-order system is fully described by ωn for speed and ζ for shape, and ζ sorts it into undamped, underdamped, critically damped and overdamped.
Peak overshoot depends on ζ alone, while peak time, rise time and settling time depend on ωn and ζ together.
Steady-state error is zero for a type-1 system with a step input and for a type-2 system with a ramp input, but a type-0 system always leaves a finite error on a step.
The static error constants K_p, K_v and K_a are just the first, second and third terms of the generalized error series, so both methods agree.
When the input is not a pure step or ramp, the dynamic error coefficients C₀, C₁, C₂, … give the error as a weighted sum of the input and its derivatives.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always ask for a derivation plus a sketch, so write the differential equation or transfer function, solve for c(t), plot it against t, and finish with the numbers in seconds and percent.

bank.q: Define the unit impulse, unit step, unit ramp and unit parabolic signals. Give the Laplace transform and a sketch of each, and explain why these four are used as standard test signals.
outline: Definition of each signal in the time domain with the interval t ≥ 0 stated
Laplace transforms 1, 1/s, 1/s², 1/s³
One sketch each, showing area of the impulse and the slopes of ramp and parabola
Reason: they are simple, repeatable, and any real input can be built from them by superposition
Impulse contains all frequencies, so it exposes the whole dynamics in one test

bank.q: Explain the terms order and type of a control system. For G(s) = 20(s + 2) / [s²(s + 5)(s + 8)] state the order, the type, and what steady-state error you expect for a step and for a ramp input.
outline: Order = number of poles of G(s), here 4
Type = number of poles at s = 0, here 2
Step input on a type-2 system: zero steady-state error
Ramp input on a type-2 system: zero steady-state error
Common mistake to avoid: counting the zero at s = −2 as a pole

bank.q: A second-order system has transfer function ωn²/(s² + 2ζωn s + ωn²). Explain how the step response changes as ζ is varied through 0, 0 < ζ < 1, ζ = 1 and ζ > 1.
outline: Poles of the characteristic equation and their location on the s-plane for each case
ζ = 0: poles on the imaginary axis, sustained oscillation at ωn
0 < ζ < 1: complex poles, oscillatory decay at frequency ωd
ζ = 1: repeated real pole, fastest non-oscillatory approach
ζ > 1: two distinct real poles, slow non-oscillatory approach
One sketch of all four responses on the same axes

bank.q: Derive the step response of a first-order system with transfer function K/(1 + τs). Show that the output reaches 63.2% of the final value at t = τ and state the values at 3τ and 4τ.
outline: C(s) = K/[s(1 + τs)] and partial fractions
c(t) = K(1 − e^(−t/τ)) for t ≥ 0
About 95% at 3τ and about 98% at 4τ
Sketch with the initial slope K/τ shown

bank.q: A unity feedback system has G(s) = 25/[s(s + 6)]. Find ωn, ζ, peak time, peak overshoot, rise time and 2% settling time, and sketch the step response.
outline: Closed-loop characteristic equation s² + 6s + 25 = 0
ωn = 5 rad/s, 2ζωn = 6 so ζ = 0.6
t_p = π/ωd ≈ 0.785 s
t_s ≈ 4/(ζωn) = 1.33 s for the 2% band
Rise time from (π − β)/ωd with β = cos⁻¹ 0.6 ≈ 0.927 rad, giving about 0.55 s

bank.q: For a unity feedback system with G(s) = K/[s(s + 2)(s + 5)], find the value of K so that the peak overshoot to a unit step is 16.3%.
outline: Peak overshoot depends only on ζ, so use M_p = e^(−πζ/√(1−ζ²))
16.3% corresponds to ζ ≈ 0.5
Characteristic equation s³ + 7s² + 10s + K = 0
Compare with the standard second-order behaviour near the dominant pole pair; the third pole is far left, so the dominant-pole approximation is acceptable
Set 2ζωn = 7 with ζ = 0.5, giving ωn = 7 rad/s, then K = 10ωn²·… by coefficient matching to give the required value
State that the approximation must be checked against the third pole position

bank.q: Determine the steady-state error of a unity feedback system with G(s) = 10/[(s + 1)(s + 4)] for a unit step, a unit ramp and a unit parabolic input. State the system type and explain the pattern in the results.
outline: Type 0 system, since no pole at the origin
K_v = lim(s→0) sG(s) = 0, so e_ss(ramp) = ∞
K_a = 0, so e_ss(parabola) = ∞
Comment: a type-0 system cannot track a ramp; one pole at the origin is needed

bank.q: A unity feedback system has open-loop transfer function G(s) = (1 + 0.5s)/[s(1 + 2s)]. Find the generalized error series for E(s)/R(s) and hence the dynamic error coefficients C₀, C₁, C₂.
outline: Substitute and simplify to a ratio of polynomials in s
Expand about s = 0 by long division or by the binomial series
Identify C₀, C₁, C₂ as the constant, s and s² coefficients
Check that C₀ equals 1/(1 + K_p) for this type-1 system, which should be zero

bank.q: The input to a unity feedback system with G(s) = 5/[s(s + 1)] is r(t) = 2 + 3t. Using the dynamic error coefficients, find the steady-state error as a function of time and its limiting value.
outline: Compute C₀ and C₁ from the expansion of s(s + 1)/[s(s + 1) + 5] about s = 0
C₀ = 0 for this type-1 system
e_ss(t) = C₀r(t) + C₁ dr/dt + (C₂/2!) d²r/dt² + …
dr/dt = 3, higher derivatives zero
Numerical value of the constant error in the same units as the input

bank.q: Compare the step responses of a first-order system and an underdamped second-order system having the same 2% settling time. Discuss which is preferable for a position control application and why.
outline: First-order response has no overshoot; settling is set by τ, with t_s ≈ 4τ
Second-order response with the same settling time must have ζωn equal to 1/τ
Smaller ζ gives faster rise but more overshoot and more control effort
Overshoot may be unacceptable where the load must not cross the set point
Conclusion: first-order-like behaviour (ζ near 0.7) is usually a good compromise

bank.q: A position control system must track a ramp input with zero steady-state error and must have a peak overshoot below 10%. Explain step by step how you would choose the system type and the damping ratio, and what trade-offs you face.
outline: Zero error on a ramp demands at least one pole at the origin, so type 1 or higher
M_p < 10% demands ζ ≥ about 0.6 from the M_p formula
Higher type improves accuracy but reduces stability margin
ωn is then chosen to meet the speed or settling-time requirement via t_s ≈ 4/(ζωn)
Gain increase raises ωn but also changes ζ; check the closed-loop poles after design
Note the conflict between accuracy and transient shape

bank.q: For a unity feedback system with G(s) = K/[s(s + a)(s + b)], examine the effect of increasing K on the transient specifications and on the steady-state error for a ramp input. Comment on the limits of increasing K.
outline: K_v = K/(ab), so ramp error falls as K rises
Closed-loop characteristic equation s³ + (a + b)s² + abs + K = 0
As K rises, the dominant pole pair becomes less damped and overshoot grows
At some K the poles cross into the right half-plane and the system becomes unstable
The third pole also moves; dominance assumption must be rechecked
Conclusion: K is bounded above by the stability and overshoot requirements

bank.q: A servomechanism is described by G(s) = 100/[s(s + 10)]. Carry out a complete time-response analysis: order and type, the closed-loop ωn and ζ, all five time-domain specifications, and the steady-state error for unit step and unit ramp inputs. State whether the design is acceptable for a positioning task.
outline: Order 2, type 1
Closed-loop characteristic equation s² + 10s + 100 = 0, giving ωn = 10 rad/s and ζ = 0.5
t_s ≈ 4/(ζωn) = 0.8 s at the 2% band; rise time from (π − β)/ωd with β = π/3
Delay time from the standard approximation
Step error zero; ramp error 1/K_v = 10/100 = 0.1
Comment: 16% overshoot may be too much; either raise ζ or add a compensator

glossary.def: The part of the response that dies away as t grows, produced by the poles of the closed-loop system.
The part of the response that remains after the transient has decayed; it has the same form as the input.
The denominator of the closed-loop transfer function set equal to zero; its roots are the closed-loop poles.
A value of s at which the transfer function becomes infinite, that is, a root of the denominator.
A value of s at which the transfer function becomes zero, that is, a root of the numerator.
lim(t→∞) f(t) = lim(s→0) sF(s), valid when all poles of sF(s) lie in the left half-plane.
A rule that turns a time function f(t) into a function F(s) of the complex variable s, converting differential equations into algebra.
Splitting a rational F(s) into simple terms whose inverse Laplace transforms are known.
A feedback loop in which H(s) = 1, so the feedback signal is the output itself.
The product G(s)H(s) around the loop with the loop opened at the summing point.
The closed-loop poles nearest the imaginary axis; they decide the shape of the transient because all other poles decay faster.
Treating a higher-order system as second order by keeping only the slowest pole pair, valid when the other poles are far to the left.
The time for the response to first reach 50% of its final value.
The amount by which the first peak exceeds the final value, expressed as a percentage of the final value.
The value of e(t) = r(t) − c(t) as t tends to infinity, written e_ss.
The signal at the summing point of a feedback loop, equal to the reference minus the fed-back output.
K_p = lim(s→0) G(s); it sets the step-input error as 1/(1 + K_p).
K_v = lim(s→0) sG(s); it sets the ramp-input error as 1/K_v.
K_a = lim(s→0) s²G(s); it sets the parabolic-input error as 1/K_a.
How closely the output follows the input long after the command is applied, measured by e_ss.
The complex plane on which poles and zeros of a transfer function are plotted, with s = σ + jω.
The loss of energy in a system that makes oscillations decay; measured by the damping ratio ζ.
